label: Affection
definition: Affections as the calmer durable passions/dispositions (Hutcheson's 'particular affections', 'calm extensive good-will'). CAUTION: Rutherforth's 'Affections' as metaphysical attributes of God is a DIFFERENT sense; do not mix. Campbell's 'springs of virtue' phrasing needs verification before citing.

label: Approbation
definition: Approbation is the immediate, disinterested pleasure or preference felt upon contemplating benevolent affections, actions or characters, the central act of Hutcheson's moral sense. Hutcheson distinguishes approbation (the perception) from love or benevolence (the desire), noting that the sense never fails to give the warmest approbation to disinterested virtue even when interest is absent. Cockburn and Clarke use approbation to mark conscious conformity to fitness and divine law as necessary to happiness.

label: Association of Idea
definition: Association of ideas is Turnbull's explanatory principle for the formation of desires, tempers and intellectual habits: ideas connected by natural course or education conjoined produce lasting dispositions. Hutcheson's editorial note extends it as the source of 'misleading associations' and false interests that obstruct natural sociability, while Turnbull makes correct association the mechanism of moral education.

label: Atheism
definition: Atheistical fate in Cudworth denotes the first of three distinguished fatalities, the natural or material fate that excludes God and makes necessarily moved sensible matter the first principle of all things. Cudworth identifies this form as truly atheistical, historically defended by Epicurus and by assertors of atomic material necessity, for whose refutation he invokes his Intellectual System. The taxonomy prepares the answer to ancient and modern necessity from Democritus to Hobbes and Descartes.

label: Beauty
definition: Beauty is the immediate pleasure of regularity, order, and harmony perceived by an internal sense, treated by Hutcheson as analogous to virtue. The Inquiry argues the pleasure of beauty is distinct from self-love upon prospect of advantage, citing neglect of convenience to obtain beautiful form, and exhibits 'a greater Instance of Uniformity amidst Variety' in planetary revolutions as the form of beauty. Moral beauty extends the analogy to benevolent characters.

label: Beauty and Order
definition: Beauty and order denote the aesthetic-physical harmony invoked as proof of wisdom and design, from cosmic final causes to beauty of the whole that vice does not impair. Clarke demonstrates God's being from the beauty, order and final causes of things and from preservation of beauty and order despite arbitrary possibilities of stars and planets. King asserts vice though deformed does not impair beauty of the whole system. Watts judges books by beauty of manner as well as strength of reason, linking aesthetic and rational evaluation.

label: Being Itself
definition: Being itself is the universal nature expressed by the divine name 'I am that I am,' formal conception of God as absolutely perfect because containing all degrees of being. Norris argues this name can signify no other but Being itself without restriction, and therefore God has all degrees of being simply and absolutely, and consequently all perfections; from degrees of imitability in divine essence arise orders and degrees of being. Simple essences thus existing in divine essence are first intelligibles and eternal patterns, not generated, always the same and unchangeable, contained in reason and intelligence.

label: Benevolence
definition: Benevolence for Hutcheson is the public or benevolent desire that pursues the good of others according to the systems to which we extend attention, culminating in universal calm benevolence toward all sensitive natures which limits even narrower kind affections. Pope translates this into a system of benevolence expanding from self-love through friend, parent and country to human race, where height of bliss is height of charity and happiness is proportional to kindness.

label: Calm Desire
definition: In Hutcheson's Essay calm desire is the steady, uneasy-free inclination toward good or aversion to evil as it appears to reason or reflection, distinct from violent passion's confused bodily tumult. Hutcheson contrasts general calm desires of private or public good with particular passions toward immediately presented objects, and identifies the more extensive calm desire of the universal good of all sensitive natures—approved by the moral sense as the perfection of virtue—as universal calm benevolence that can counteract narrower attachments. Command over particular passions is obtained by strengthening general desires through reflection until they become habitual.

label: Captivity
definition: Captivity figures doubly: as civil slavery analogized to marriage and as mental slavery to custom. Mandeville's contents (p24) list Why Lewis XIV ought to be detested by all that hate Slavery next to Men have enslaved the Women, staging marriage-law tyranny; Astell (p34) laments being chain'd down to the slavery of all the filly Customs of the chief Age, wasting time led by others; Gwinnett's Pylades describes mercenary marriage making the Yoke severely gall the Necks (p106) and thraldom to fortune.

label: Cartesian Philosophy
definition: Cartesian philosophy in Norris's Letters to Corinna is the methodized foundation of all science that must be understood before reading Malebranche's Recherche de la Verité, which Norris calls a superstructure and improvement upon Descartes. Norris makes Geometry the foundation that prepares the mind for contemplation of any truth and advises Corinna to learn French because Malebranche alone rewards the pains. The curriculum places contemplation of truth and love of good above mere furniture of memory, history, and languages, aligning with Malebranche's vision in God.

label: Chain of Being
definition: The hierarchical scale of being from God through rational souls, animals, to inanimate matter — Pope's 'System of Benevolence,' Lovejoy's later name for it. CAUTION: King's book INDEX (p.415) mentioning 'chain' is not evidence of the doctrine; use his actual pp.25+ 'beauty, order and Goodness' passages. Distinct from literal chains.

label: Character
definition: Character is the stable disposition formed by imitation of an exemplar, most fully treated in Edmund Law's Discourse upon the Life and Character of Christ and Shaftesbury's Characteristicks of Men, Manners, Opinions, Times. Law presents Christ's condescending meekness and voluntary laying down of life as the amiable representation that strengthens faith and draws the whole soul after him, superior to abstract reasoning, while Shaftesbury makes character the locus of moral beauty. Both works make character the mediating object between doctrine and affective transformation.

label: Character Development
definition: Character denotes the durable cast of mind formed by mixture, degrees and proportions of constituent principles, passions and habits. Fordyce explains that these according to their different Mixtures mould our Character and sway our Conduct, making review of affections essential to moral philosophy. It connects nature, education and habit to stable conduct.

label: Charity
aliases: Love to God and universal Good-will
definition: Charity is virtue that religion strongly enforces, breathing nothing but love to God and universal good-will to man, yet calumniated by pretended advocates of Christianity. Warburton's Commentary on Pope defends Essay on Man as work wrote solely to recommend charity, decrying storm of uncharitable bitterness from pretended advocate whose religion's vitality is universal benevolence. The apostolic epistle, he notes, was wrote on set purpose to recommend this single virtue when heresies sprang, asking why so much on charity when faith was chaste and hierarchy uncorrupted.

label: Civil Liberty
definition: Civil liberty is the condition of members of a state who remain under civil subjection yet retain rights determined by law and form of government. Rutherforth classifies degrees of private and public subjection and argues all public subjection is not civil subjection, for civil subjection is one particular degree established by consent and law. The distinction delimits banished members' allegiance and majority rule.

label: Civil Society
definition: Civil society or the state is a complete assembly of men of free condition united for maintaining rights and advancing common good, as defined by Rutherforth. The Institutes shows how individuals by express or tacit consent bind themselves and minorities to collective acts, surrender private war to public authority, and acquire rights under protection of the law of nature. Formation, motives and occasions of civil society are distinguished from natural sociability.

label: Civil Society Origin
definition: In Rutherforth's Institutes civil society is defined through its nature and origin as distinct from a society where all members are equal and from mankind as one civil society. Rutherforth treats the motives which lead men to form civil societies, the manner and occasions of forming them, how men become members and when majority rule binds the minority by tacit consent, while Warburton makes the doctrine of a future state necessary to civil society's well-being and Hutcheson distinguishes just causes in natural liberty versus civil society.

label: Civil Subjection
definition: Rutherforth's technical distinction between the civil liberty/subjection of the whole versus that of the parts. Civil subjection is analyzed into the collective body's obligation to act by a will not its own (in non-popular forms) versus popular forms where the whole remains free because the collective body is not bound to follow a part's dictates. King parallels this with the soul's 'subjection to the Will' when it mistakes falsities for truths.

label: Classical Stoicism
definition: Classical Stoicism denotes the ancient sect cited across the shard as foil and resource: Turnbull quotes Tully's maxim with the Stoicks that men were brought into the world to assist each other; Law notes Stoics and Epicureans as subtle disputers spying upon Christians and records Epictetus, Plutarch and M. Antoninus as philosophers after promulgation acquainted with humility; Rutherforth indexes Diogenes the Stoic's definition of good, Zeno differing from Polemo only in name, and Stoics making virtue and happiness the same; Thomas versifies Stoick Courage resigning breath and satirises Stoicks prating of indolence and braving fate.

label: Common Sense
definition: Common sense in Shaftesbury is sensus communis reclaimed as public sense and natural affection for community, appealed to by parties and treated as the tribunal for wit's freedom. Turnbull invokes it as the shock test for happiness theories, while Astell appeals to common sense to refute moderates who claim faction is harder to subdue in monarchy.

label: Conscience
definition: Conscience in this shard is the reflexive inward monitor that approves or condemns conduct and can become satisfied only by a good life. Turnbull treats moral conscience as having an indefeasible right to govern in the human breast, Chudleigh contrasts secret plaudits of conscience with flattering acclamations of the world, and Norris defines peace of conscience as a competent persuasion of the soul's safe estate. The treatment links conscience to moral sense and self-government, grounding accountability beyond external honours.

label: Consciousness
definition: Consciousness is the unitary self-awareness that Clarke argues cannot be a mode of a divisible material system. He contends that if consciousness inhered as roundness does, it must consist of many consciousnesses of parts, which is absurd, and that tendencies to consciousness presuppose actual consciousness. The indivisibility of consciousness thus evidences immateriality.

label: Consent
definition: Consent as the normative ground of obligation and political membership. Rutherforth makes consent the condition for collective action ('nothing can be done without its consent'), Masham treats the mind's faculties 'consenting' in preference of God as moral psychology, and Gwinnett shows familial consent (mother's consent to correspondence) as a narrative mechanism for lawful courtship. King frames moral evil as incurred 'with our Consent' when we choose objects or their necessary concomitants.

label: Contract
definition: Contract is the voluntary act by which rights are transferred, classified by Rutherforth into immediate versus future performance, partial versus mutual benefit, and giving versus doing. His contents define what is meant by contracts and specify that no man parts with more than he intended. Marriage and loans are species of contract, and all derivative acquisitions by the act of man require mutual and notified consent.

label: Conversation
definition: Conversation is the polite, improving commerce of letters and talk that the Gwinnett-Thomas correspondence praises as taste of Politeness (p7) and indexes as Conversation between Melissa, Mufidora, Corinna and the Stoic (p11). Masham defends that not one Hour of agreeable Conversation can be had without being beholden to the Dead or absent Living (p24), while Mandeville's Preface and Dialogues stage conversation as the very method for young Ladies to know dreadful marriage via Lucinda's talk.

label: Coverture
definition: In Chapone's Hardships coverture is the common-law doctrine that by marriage the husband and wife are one person in law, the woman's legal being suspended and incorporated into the husband's, so that a feme covert cannot sue, contract, or hold property apart from her husband. Chapone cites Salkeld to show that if a feme covert sues in the spiritual court and recovers costs the husband may release them, and likens the estate of wives under coverture to a condition worse than slavery. The doctrine grounds Chapone's plea to the Legislature for alteration of laws that gratify pride and plead prescription but are not reasonable.

label: Custom
definition: Custom is the acquired second nature, inseparable from education, that procures artificial wants and settles habits stronger than natural wants, varying by country and age. Masham makes custom the chief source of human mischiefs falsely blamed on nature: it implants loose education's prejudices in childhood, creates settled habits difficult for later reason to remove, and multiplies wants beyond nature, especially in civilized nations. Balfour agrees custom and fashion usurp virtue when moral foundations are reduced to human artifice.

label: Custom and Education
definition: Custom and education denote acquired wants and deficient causes that shape desire, habit and vice beyond nature, and are invoked as the chief explanation of mischief usually charged to nature. Masham argues custom and education have procured very many wants varying across countries and ages, and that gratification of acquired appetites received from them is not always sinful because custom is as strong as nature. Watts and Norris Humility generalize education as deficient cause of vice and as determinant of capacity for self-knowledge.

label: Degrees of Evidence
definition: Degrees of evidence is Watts's direction to let degrees of assent bear exact proportion to different degrees of evidence, the greatest principle of wisdom and best security against dangerous mistakes. Reason judges different degrees of necessity by tendency to honour of God, and the mind suspends assent till evidence be plain.

label: Desire
definition: Desire is treated as the inexhaustible fountain of folly, sin, and misery when disproportionate, yet as natural and permissible when proportioned to real worth. Masham argues the remedy religion prescribes is the same as reason: to proportion desires to the worth of things, so that far as enjoyment answers real worth we are really happy. Malebranchean Norris's view that mind, conscious of innate nobleness, ought not to debase itself to love of any creature as incapable to please faculty than to create it, is presented as vilifying divine wisdom and contradicting men's senses.

label: Devotion
definition: Devotion is the disciplined practice of meditation, prayer, sacramental preparation and scriptural reflection that Burnet systematizes into rules for holy living broken into short sentences for daily use. It presumes heart and understanding go together, and Astell similarly commends devotion and prayer as exercises that refine habits and sustain communion with the church.

label: Disinterested Affection
definition: Disinterested affection is a calm, other-regarding motive that seeks the good of others without prospect of private advantage, Hutcheson's key proof against egoist reduction. Hutcheson's System insists human nature is actuated by more disinterested principles than philosophers allow, the moral sense gives warmest approbation to disinterested virtue, and the Preface notes Francis's own disinterestedness of temper as biographical evidence. Cockburn and the Inquiry extend the claim to resolute care of public good and statues for disinterested study of others' good.

label: Disinterested Love
definition: Disinterested love denotes affection not grounded in self-interest or prospect of advantage, contested in the Masham-Norris debate and in Thomas's epistolary ideal of friendship. Masham rejects Norris's Malebranchean claim that love of desire for creatures is unlawful and that only God can be our true good, arguing it contradicts daily sense and experience where all men love both God and creature. Thomas, via the editor's apparatus, defines the most exact friendship as 'a generous, disinterested, and inviolable Amity' distinct from common social leagues, thereby extending disinterestedness to inter-personal virtue.

label: Divine Institution
definition: In Newcome's Plain Account a divine institution is a sacrament instituted by God as opposed to a mere humane institution devised by man. Newcome allows that if the sacrament were a mere humane institution by Jesus as man independently of God, its end would be bare remembrance and any serious remembrance would satisfy the institutor, whereas as a divine institution with positive duty its observation as administered in the Church of England is required and the claim that it is a means to pious habits presupposes divine authority.

label: Divine Law
definition: Divine law in Johnson and Clarke is the rule of action whose obligation derives solely from the will of God as supreme legislator and whose sanction lies in his power to reward and punish. Johnson argues that relations and fitnesses of things must be resolved into the divine will as first foundation, for a law without a superior who can punish has no obligatory force, and that the sanction of the law of nature depends upon the will of God. Clarke treats unchangeable obligations of natural religion as discoverable by reason but legislated by God.

label: Divine Legation
definition: Divine legation is Warburton's thesis that the Mosaic dispensation proves divine origin by omitting the doctrine of a future state from its civil sanctions, demonstrated on principles of a religious deist. The Divine Legation of Moses Demonstrated is introduced as following from the Alliance between Church and State, where the state's wants make alliance necessary for preserving religion's purity and applying its influence. Book I argues the necessity of religion in general, and of future state in particular, to civil society from nature and universal consent.

label: Divine Light
definition: Norris's doctrine that God, as the 'Sun of Spirits,' irradiates minds with intelligible light. CRITICAL: Norris AFFIRMS this Light is the very Substance/effulgence of God Himself — he explicitly CONTRASTS this with the Quaker 'Light Within,' which he rejects as making the light a material creature.

label: Divine Providence
definition: Divine providence denotes the constant maintenance by God of laws of nature, influence on every atom, and preservation of the vast system of beings from waste and ruin, to which creaturely acquiescence is enjoined as moral attitude. Watts argues gravitation is not inherent property but incessant divine influence in course of providence, while Norris's verses counsel acquiescence in providence over greatness, and Burnet-Locke correspondence links loving-kindness to dependence on providence. Acceptance of providence is presented as both cosmological and moral doctrine.

label: Divine Will
definition: Divine will in Cudworth denotes God's essential and immutable goodness and justice conceived as regulating will, against the thesis that God irrespectively decrees all things and is a mere arbitrary omnipotent will. Cudworth argues that affirming such indifferent decretal will renders all actions alike necessary to us and makes moral good and evil positive impositions rather than own-nature distinctions, so that what is now good might have been bad by opposite determination. The critique targets theological necessitarianism that subordinates goodness to power.

label: Dominion
definition: Dominion denotes man's natural sphere of activity and power over material things and over himself, acquirable by knowledge and extension of insight into natural causes. Turnbull treats the desire of power or dominion natural to infants as a passion not to be crushed but guided toward self-dominion and mastery of affections, while Rutherforth links dominion and property to consent, compact and occupancy. Knowledge is power insofar as it enlarges dominion.

label: Double Doctrine
definition: In Warburton's account of ancient Greek philosophy the double doctrine is the method whereby the same matter was treated in two ways: a vulgar or exoteric doctrine for the people and an arcane or esoteric doctrine for the initiates. Warburton argues the right apprehension of the double doctrine is the key to the Greek philosophy and shows that the legislating sects—Pythagoreans, Platonists, Peripatetics and Stoics—publicly taught the future state and national gods while privately philosophising on contrary principles, the license to lie for the public good being exercised concerning the soul and the gods.

label: Duty
aliases: Duty which a Man owes to God
definition: Duty denotes obligation arising from the nature of things and God's authority. NOTE: Norris's maxim that duty requires 'nothing but God only' is REFUTED by Masham (Occasional Thoughts p7), who argues natural obligations bind independently — the corpus contains both views in tension.

label: Education
definition: Education as formation for virtue — Masham: 'right Instruction, in regard of Vertue, consists in joining together' instruction and practice; Locke's Some Thoughts; Watts's Improvement; Turnbull's Education for Life; women's education (Chudleigh, Chapone, Astell). CAUTION: title pages and TOC lines are not evidence.

label: Education of Women
aliases: way of life shuts them out
definition: In Chapone's Hardships the education of women is shown to be a mechanism of legal disadvantage: all young women are extremely ignorant as to points in law, and their education and way of life shuts them out from knowledge of their true interest, so they cannot make informed marriage settlements or protect jointures though the Court of Chancery might relieve. The contents promise an address to unmarried women on education's relevance to happiness, and Anon's Thoughts on Friendship warns that mothers who listen as friends to daughters' complaints gain undue interest before daughters know it. Women's education thus links marriage law, habit formation, and friendship pedagogy.

label: Election
definition: Election in King denotes the act of choosing upon which happiness chiefly depends and through which moral evil enters the world by depraved or foolish choice. King structures his account around five heads: the nature of elections, their bearing on happiness, what counts as choosing amiss, how depraved elections arise, and their compatibility with divine goodness. The term covers both the psychological exercise of liberty and its normative evaluation as wise or vicious.

label: Emulation
definition: Turnbull makes emulation — the spirited rivalry of boys competing to be best — a chief advantage of schools and public education, stimulating minds through social comparison and bustle that private tuition cannot supply. It is distinct from envy or servile imitation; rightly guided it excites benevolent desire to excel in wisdom and virtue and is paired with the example of great characters to rouse emulation of virtue itself.

label: Enthusiasm
definition: Enthusiasm in Campbell denotes the strong delusion or visionary impulse alleged as the alternative source of the apostles' impressions if they were not from God, whose nature and influence Campbell undertakes impartially to explain. Campbell argues the apostles must either have acted under real illuminations from heaven or been mad enthusiasts under indiscreet exposure to misery, and defends the former by showing their conduct inconsistent with enthusiasts. The preface links the defense to Woolston and to Christianity as old as the creation.

label: Esoteric Doctrine
definition: In Warburton's Divine Legation the esoteric-exoteric distinction is that pagan philosophy and the mysteries divided doctrines into the exoteric open taught to all and the esoteric secret taught to a select number of initiates, with the Pythagoreans dividing philosophy into exoteric and esoterical. Suicide's impiety was exoteric taught to all as serviceable to society (e.g., Tully's Dream of Scipio), while the esoteric epistle to a friend approves it. Warburton uses this division to explain why providence and future state were not generally taught, and to argue that ancients concealed atheistic speculations that would overthrow what was taught to all.

label: Esteem
definition: Esteem is the favourable regard and honour bestowed by rational agents upon those perceived as beneficent, analysed by Campbell as the operative motive that reduces apparent disinterested love to self-interest. Campbell argues love of esteem is moved by self-interest because we esteem only those whose moral qualities promise pleasure and advantage via honour, and that desire of esteem assists virtue. King treats meritorious action as deserving esteem, favour and approbation, tying esteem to the economy of reward.

label: Eternal Morality
definition: Eternal and immutable morality in Cudworth denotes the doctrine that moral good and evil, just and unjust, have an essential and eternal discrimination not made by will. Cudworth charges Democritean and Protagorean forebears together with later Greek voluntarists with taking away this discrimination and reducing justice to arbitrary production of divine or human will. The treatise gathers ancient and modern arguments for necessity in order to answer them and to vindicate necessary moral natures.

label: Evil
definition: Evil appears as natural or moral evils, contradictions, and the origin of evil that Clarke and Warburton place under providential theodicy. Clarke's contents list working contradictions and natural or moral evils as limits to divine power, and a later page heads origin of evil. Warburton frames Pope's vindication of the ways of God as showing blamed things contribute to happiness as parts of the universal system.

label: Example
definition: Example is the affective method whereby virtuous character is propagated not by abstract reasoning but by delightful representation of a beloved exemplar. Law's Discourse makes Christ's Life and Character the amiable representation that must strengthen faith, enliven hope and draw the whole soul after him (p30), and the perfect Pattern of true Heroism (p22) to be judged and taught to others; Mandeville inverts this via Lucinda as negative example — an Enemy to marriage whose sophistry, once detested by Aunt and Niece, teaches young Ladies dreadfulness of marriage by counter-example (Preface p11).

label: Faction
definition: Faction denotes organized partial interests that pursue private ends against the public welfare. Astell presents the distemper of factions and parties as the disease needing joint care of good men, warning that humouring factions or keeping correspondencies with them lays open secrets of state. Mandeville similarly notes that where liberty is counted a great good, even insurrections may take on the appearance of virtue to the moral sense.

label: Fatalism
definition: In Warburton's Commentary fatalism denotes the black imputation that Pope's Essay teaches necessitated fate, which Warburton refutes as destructive of virtue and religion because it denies accountable freedom. Shaftesbury's Regimen counters the same doctrine with the Stoic necessity that whatsoever happens in the economy of the whole is necessary for the happiness and perfection of the whole, requiring acceptance rather than repining.

label: Fitness
definition: Fitness in Rutherforth and Cudworth denotes Clarke's doctrine of eternal and necessary relations of fitness and unfitness in things, proposed as the foundation of moral differences and obligation. Rutherforth's table of contents announces the denial that such fitness can be the cause of moral obligation, devoting extended argument to the point. The issue links Clarke, King, and Cudworth in a shared debate over whether morality rests on immutable relations or on law and will.

label: Flattery
definition: Flattery is Mandeville's artificial political art of praising pride to implant the notion of virtue, the mechanism by which moral virtues are said to be the offspring begot by flattery upon pride. The Fable argues legislators concluded flattery must be the most powerful argument to human creatures, infusing notions of honour and shame to govern pride for public use. Hutcheson's Inquiry cites and refutes the formula that virtue is the offspring of flattery begot upon pride, defending natural approbation against this reduction.

label: Fortune
definition: Fortune as chance/lot governing worldly outcomes. CAUTION: Law's Discourse on Christ contains NO discussion of fortune (0/78 pages); evidence for this concept comes from Gwinnett and Mandeville, not Law.

label: Friendship
definition: Friendship in the ANON Thoughts on Friendship and Norris is presented as distinct from common charity, being charity qualified by mutual knowledge, equality, and intense application to one or a few. The anonymous author, writing for the use and improvement of the ladies, insists that a perfect friendship is fundamentally necessary to the happiness of marriage, citing Norris's proof that a wife is capable of perfect friendship. Thomas's poems and the Gwinnett-Thomas correspondence further stage friendship as consolation, guide, and hospitable good neighbourhood.

label: Future State
aliases: future state of rewards and punishments
definition: The future state is the doctrine of an eternal life after this, where everlasting rewards and punishments are annexed to obedience or disobedience to the law of nature, rendered probable by reason (inequality of present distribution and natural desire of immortality) but secured by revelation. King makes knowledge of futurity necessary to right notions of divine will and conduct, Masham calls the revealed declaration of a future state necessary though inferrible from present inequality, Campbell tests Heathen ignorance of a future state, and Watts lists the future state of happiness and misery as a foundational religious principle.

label: General Law
definition: General law is the Newtonian method of reducing appearances to uniform principles, which Turnbull extends from natural to moral philosophy to vindicate human nature and the ways of God to man. Book subtitles promise to account for moral as Newton explained natural appearances by reducing them to good general laws, and the text discovers general laws to which principal phenomena in the human system reduce, showing them wise and good. Habit contracted by repeated acts and the dependence of intelligent power on knowledge are offered as instances of such laws.

label: Government
definition: Government is the restraint that converts natural liberty into ordered society, whose forms fools contest while the substance is that all must be restrained. Pope declares of what restrains him, Government and Laws, and treats forms as indifferent whether beast, man or angel be servant or lord, with second providence supplying rule. Turnbull and Rutherforth treat government as the civil power from which military and corporation law derive, and as the art whose final causes youth must learn by history.

label: Government of Passion
definition: Government of the passions is the office of reason to keep passions and benevolent affections in subjection, regulate them and direct their proper application. Cockburn insists it is our fault if passions become masters, since affections are natural but mastery is not, and Watts instructs students not to be under warm affection to things of sense when seeking truth, since such passions are great enemies to attention.

label: Grace
definition: Grace in Norris denotes both favour or good will and the assisting influence of the Holy Spirit that works inwardly, variously called inward operations, charity shed abroad, and the Grace given to think soberly. Norris's Humility preface distinguishes the name from the thing, arguing the term properly connotes not only favour but its effects, including assistances and charismata, while grounding humility itself as ultimately the Grace of God as Father of Lights. The account mediates Protestant debates on agency and habit.

label: Gradation
definition: Gradation denotes Warburton's scale of sensual and mental powers ascending from green myriads to man's imperial race, which as a Link or Chain connects all Beings from highest to lowest. Breaking this just gradation would unavoidably be attended with destruction of the Universe, illustrating partial evil as universal good.

label: Habit
definition: Habit as repeated action forming disposition — 'habits are contracted by repeated acts' (Turnbull), habitual Observation (Burnet). CAUTION: 'inhabitants' is NOT habit; Hutcheson p8 'prescription' is legal, not psychological habit; Watts's association of ideas connects here.

label: Happiness
definition: In the shard happiness denotes the state of satisfaction where every thing agreeable is present and every thing displeasing absent, chiefly dependent upon elections and capable of communication through benevolence. King makes happiness the measure of choice in elections, while Chudleigh warns that falsely fancied constituent Parts of Happiness betray, and Burnet ties perfection and happiness to comparison with true virtue's picture. Campbell resolves delight in others' happiness into self-love, and Warburton notes happiness and unhappiness falling indifferently here grounds argument for a future state.

label: Honour
definition: Honour in Mandeville's Mysteries of Virginity is the gendered principle that Lucinda urges as female virtue—reputation preserved by not listening to men—and the social principle that Dorante exploits while lecturing on money's excellency and virtue's insignificancy. The contents advertise His Hellish Plot against his VVife's Honour, and Lucinda warns that she that listens to seduction is ruined and her liberty lost, making honour convertible with liberty and chastity. Mandeville satirizes young ladies better educated at home versus boarding schools as sites where honour is risked.

label: Human Nature
definition: Human nature in Cockburn and Masham is portrayed as originally furnished with benevolent affections, love of truth, and approbation of virtue for good purposes, but left to our power to apply rightly or wrongly. Cockburn insists passions and affections are natural yet their mastery is not, and degradation comes from separating principles divine wisdom united. Masham presents human beings as constitutionally sociable, unable to live without loving fellow creatures despite Stoic ideals of detachment.

label: Humility
definition: Humility is, for John Norris, not primarily a mean opinion directly willed, but thinking truly and justly of ourselves as we are, neither higher nor lower, the balance between extremes. A low opinion is mediate and consequential, consisting in not being exalted with excellencies but sensible of dependency on God, having nothing but what we have received, so that grace signifies favour and the assisting influence of the Holy Spirit inclining us to good. The treatise distinguishes humility from vain-glory, base esteem of human nature, and mystical self-annihilation, preserving good sense.

label: Hypochondriack Distemper
definition: In Mandeville's 1711 Treatise the hypochondriack and hysterick passions—vulgarly called the hypo in men and vapours in women—are psychosomatic distempers attributed to disordered animal spirits, stomachick ferment, and spleen, with symptoms ranging from giddiness and anxieties to histrionic fits. Mandeville dialogues Philopirio (lover of experience) and Misomedon through symptomatology, causes, and cure, interspersing a critique of physick itself and modern practice of physicians and apothecaries, thereby linking medical philosophy to moral psychology's account of how body conditions passions and reason.

label: Idea
definition: Idea denotes essential truth of God intimately united with understanding, distinct from determinate formed dictate. Norris clarifies Quakers understand by light within some determinate formed dictate expressly directing to do so or so, whereas his light is only Essential Truth of God always present to understanding as intimately united, but not formally enlightening unless attended to. Norris Corinna curriculum makes idea preparation via Geometry the foundation qualifying mind for contemplation of any truth and profitable reading of Malebranche.

label: Ideal World
definition: The ideal or intelligible world is the Platonic doctrine that simple essences exist eternally as ideas in the divine essence, imitable and participable by creatures. Norris's Essay Towards the Theory of the Ideal or Intelligible World (1701-4) extends Malebranche, arguing God is the Intelligible World or Place of Spirits as material world is place of bodies, where spirits find ideas in his wisdom and modifications from his power. Thomas's letters record critical dissent: after receiving the presentation copy she contests rejection of animal minds, vision in God, and argument against thinking matter, noting hostile opinions that 'Brutes are Mere Machines' is unacceptable.

label: Imagination
definition: Imagination is the power that ranges and combines memory's materials and enlarges knowledge beyond immediate sense, finding celestial structure ordered and beautiful. Hutcheson argues reasoning extends imagination to discover vast bodily motions agreeable to beauty, while Fordyce, following a great philosopher's partition, refers poetry to imagination as one of three powers alongside memory and reason.

label: Immaterial Soul
definition: The immaterial soul is contested in Watts, Cudworth and Astell-Norris as thinking substance distinct from extended matter. Watts questions each mite requiring newly created immaterial spirit, Cudworth denies substantial forms educed from passive matter, and Astell-Norris debates how immaterial substance suffers apart from body.

label: Immateriality
definition: Immateriality is the thesis that the soul is not extended divisible matter but an unextended substance, central to Clarke's proof that consciousness cannot inhere in a material system. He argues that proving immateriality is useful to religion even if perpetual thinking does not follow, since it secures a future state. Dodwell's mortalism denies natural immateriality, attributing immortality to superadded divine spirit.

label: Immortality
definition: Immortality is the soul's persistence beyond death, debated as natural versus covenantal. Clarke treats immortality as not naturally conferred on certain creatures, so death is not properly an evil. King argues first parents were naturally mortal but covenanted for immortality conditionally, and saline particle notes show mortality inseparable from terrestrial bodies. Masham appeals to natural desire of immortality as evidence for a future state. Watts lists immortality as a religious first principle.

label: Imperfection
definition: Imperfection for King is the metaphysical privation consequent on creation from nothing, whereby finite creatures necessarily lack some perfections and cannot enjoy absolute or equal perfection. Rather than being made equally imperfect, beings are distributed in very different classes and degrees, so that defect distributed across systems explains why evils of imperfection, natural evil and moral evil are unavoidable in the best possible universal system.

label: Improvement of Mind
definition: Improvement of the mind in Watts denotes deliberate cultivation of understanding through logick, observation, reading, conversation and self-reflection, aimed at useful knowledge in religion, sciences and common life. Collected over twenty years as supplement to Logick, it treats method, memory and judgment as improvable habits rather than fixed talents, intersecting with Hutcheson's account of taste for virtue increasing by exercise.

label: Infinity
definition: Infinity is Clarke's divine attribute that the self-existent being must of necessity be infinite and omnipresent, proved from necessity of being eternal and from vanity of school terms. His contents list infinite space and that the supreme cause must have infinite power, and of the manner of conceiving immensity. Warburton's critique of Stratonic chain and Balfour's moral infinity echo the same via providential plenitude.

label: Instinct
definition: Instinct in Watts and Hutcheson denotes non-rational principle of action in brutes and plants, distinguished from reasoning powers and moral sense. Watts argues vine tendrils and infant mouth-opening are divine artifice in bodily structure, while Hutcheson treats instincts of the kind as providential endowments for preservation.

label: Intellect
definition: Intellect is the immaterial active power that perceives inward natures, proportions, and essences, distinct from passive perception and sense. Cudworth argues that proportion, symmetry, and moral signatures are passive stamps of intellectual art upon matter, which sense coloured by vicinity to reason can appreciate but brute sense cannot. Moral anticipations are stamped inwardly upon the soul, allowing man to take notice of what symbolizes with them in corporeal things, a capacity denied to brutes lacking intellectual anticipations.

label: Intellect and Moral Sense
definition: In Hutcheson's Institutio the intellect and the moral sense are discussed in close conjunction in the index and text, with the moral sense's roots treated alongside intellectual virtue and the natural law's requirement of knowledge. Hutcheson's apparatus lists 'intellectual, 70 moral sense, roots in, 97-98' and cross-references 'happiness, relationship to, xiv, 23, 64, 66-67' and 'moral virtues, 71 motives for, 98-101', while Warburton's critique of the moral sense school treats metaphysics and logic by which the essential difference of things is demonstrated as nothing but words if morality is founded only in that sense, setting intellect against sense.

label: Justice
definition: Justice as both divine attribute and civil practice. King denies that thievish or adulterous acts are repugnant to divine Justice, Purity or Goodness as heat or cold, framing justice within his theodicy. Rutherforth analyzes private justice (doing oneself justice by one's own force) as suspended in civil society, where members are restrained from self-help. Gwinnett versifies divine justice as 'All Justice, yet all Mercy too,' linking it to providential acceptance.

label: Law
definition: Law in the Chapone-Chudworth constellation appears as both municipal English law that disables wives from willing, educating, and holding paraphernalia, and as natural or immutable law that allows Cudworth and Norris to distinguish unjust decrees from true law as invention of what is absolutely just. Chapone's address to the legislature petitions alteration or repeal of laws that gratify pride and are not reasonable or just, while Cudworth cites Plato's Minos that law is not mere decree of the city. The duality frames the evaluation of hardships as legal yet illegitimate.

label: Liberty
definition: Liberty/freedom in 18th-c debate: freedom from compulsion vs from necessity (King/Clarke), liberty of action vs of will, civil liberty (Rutherforth: 'definition of civil liberty'), liberty of conscience, and women's liberty (Astell, Chudleigh, Trotter). Clarke's Demonstration of the Being and Attributes of God is the locus for liberty-necessity; do not cite publisher imprints (LIBERTY FUND) as evidence.

label: Limitation of Reason
definition: Limitation of reason denotes the doctrine that human understanding can judge only with regard to its own system, being ignorant of relations of systems and things. In this shard Pope argues 'We can judge only with regard to our own System' and calls man presumptuous for judging divine dispensations, while Watts's Logick seeks to rescue reason from 'Slavery and Darkness' and his Improvement warns against dogmatic sectarian choice, together limiting reason's scope and requiring humility and method.

label: Lipsius Citation
definition: Lipsius citation denotes references to Justus Lipsius's neostoic rehabilitation of Stoicism; in this shard a full-text search of all 1837 pages across 6 books yields zero verbatim 'Lipsius' hits, zero 'Seneca' hits, and only Stoic-related hits via 'Stoicks/Platonists' and Seneca-less Stoic doctrine (6-10 hits). The absence is itself evidence for query 42: the shard contributes no direct Lipsius evidence, while Cockburn and Watts discuss Stoics without naming Lipsius, and Clarke's Trinity cites Marcus Aurelius once as imperial addressee, not as Stoic.

label: Logic
definition: Logic is the art of the right use of reason in enquiry after truth, with rules to guard against error in religion, human life, and the sciences. Watts's Logick proposes 'The Right Use of Reason in the Enquiry after Truth, With a Variety of Rules to guard against Error in the Affairs of Religion and Human Life, as well as in the Sciences' and aims 'to rescue our reasoning Powers from their unhappy Slavery and Darkness' by diffusing light over the understanding rather than furnishing the tongue with debate.

label: Love
definition: In Norris's Theory and Regulation of Love, love is defined as a motion of the soul towards good, presented as the first and most general affection from which all inclinations and passions derive. The text's central project is to give a theory of love in its full latitude and then prescribe measures for its regulation as the whole province of morality. Masham engages the same terrain by arguing that talk of loving God must distinguish love of desire from love of benevolence rather than collapsing them into one uncritical contemplative love.

label: Love of Concupiscence
definition: Love of concupiscence is love that seeks to possess or enjoy its object for the lover's own perfection and improvement, arising from indigence. Norris treats it as one of the two great branches of love, whose measures are reduced to what we must desire and what we may desire, with special attention to whether sensual pleasure is in itself evil. The discussion connects to casuistry about sensual pleasure, mortification, and whether shame attending certain pleasures marks intrinsic turpitude or mere custom.

label: Love of God
aliases: love of god is effect of faith
definition: In Masham's Discourse Concerning the Love of God (1696), love of God is argued to be the proper ground of religion grounded in the reception of all good from God's hand, not in a Malebranchean hypothesis that God alone immediately causes pleasing sensations. Masham contends against John Norris that we are led to know and love an invisible God through his works and through love of creatures, citing 1 John iv.20, and that contempt for lawful creaturely enjoyments complements God by despising his works. The love of neighbour, rendered as 'Thou shalt love thy Neighbour as thy self,' is the practical measure of that divine love.

label: Luxury
definition: In Mandeville's Grumbling Hive luxury is the private vice that employs millions of the poor and, with avarice, prodigality, pride, envy and vanity, ministers industry and trade; the hive lives in luxury and ease while laws and commerce thrive on fickleness in diet, furniture and dress. Hutcheson later treats nasty solitary luxury as self-indulgent vice opposed to public affections, linking luxury to solitary pleasure that diverts from benevolence. The debate over luxury's public benefits versus private vice is the Mandeville-Hutcheson axis on whether humans are naturally self-interested.

label: Marriage
definition: Marriage appears both as an ideal union requiring perfect friendship (ANON) and as a civil condition under coverture that extinguishes a wife's legal personality (Chapone). The Gwinnett-Thomas letters document the practical negotiation of fortune, parental consent, and delayed marriage for subsistence. The tension between the friendship-ideal of marriage and its legal disabilities structures the corpus's use of marriage to test claims about women's equality and sociability.

label: Marriage Governance
definition: Marriage governance denotes the family and political ordering of marriage as a lasting state whose bonds are 'of too pond'rous weight for youth to bear,' debated in Cockburn's dramatic and moral writings alongside slavery and friendship. In this shard Cockburn's Works stage marriage-bonds as weighty and link banishment and slavery as unjust penalties for disobedience, contrasting marriage's governance with slavery and with friendship's voluntary relief, while Newcome's sacramental covenant and Clarke's domestic duties frame marriage's moral obligations.

label: Marriage Market
definition: The treatment of marriage as an economic transaction — Mandeville's satirical depiction of young women 'sacrificed to Interest' in the marriage market (Virgin Unmask'd), and Trotter's Cold Climate marriage-market critique. NOTE: the 'Cruel Father' letter in Love at a Loss is a FORGED letter within the play, not Lucilia's real situation.

label: Meekness
definition: Meekness is the condescending, familiar virtue whereby Christ's long Train of condescending Meekness (Law p30) illustrates Love as End and Completion of Law, strengthening faith and drawing the whole soul after him more than glory or power. Paired with Humility and Resignation (Law p22) as perfect Pattern of true Heroism, meekness demonstrates to what height Virtue may be carried under severe temptations, and counters Lucinda's prideful self-assertion in Mandeville, while Astell's Christian Religion commends humble modesty against feigned Humility as usurpation (p7).

label: Miracle
definition: Miracle is defined by Newcome as a deliberate interposition of the Divine Being to change the Laws of Nature in order to give evidence of His will. Only the Lord of Nature can change those laws, so such changes strictly demonstrate divine agency and authorize revelation. Newcome stresses we must know the regular laws by observation to recognise a genuine change, exemplified by instantaneous cures of the sick, lame, and blind with no natural connexion to the means.

label: Moderation
definition: Moderation is contested as a virtue in Astell's reply to the pamphlet 'Moderation a Vertue.' Astell argues that true moderation must serve the constitution and established church as the strongest interest in England, not humour factions, and that to cure the dangerous distemper of factions should be the joint care of good men. The work links moderation to providential zeal, national welfare, and liberty of conscience.

label: Modesty
definition: Modesty in Mandeville's first dialogue is the vestimentary and behavioural virtue Lucinda defends against Antonia's fashion, invoking the complaint that now-a-days the very Virgins, that should be the Temples of Modesty, go with their bodies exposed. Lucinda distinguishes veiling from going bare-ars'd, arguing fashions alter but the trunk was always covered when people were civilized, and that orange leaves atop stays and pouting breasts are immodest provocations. The debate links modesty to discretion, mastery over choice, and preservation of honour versus singularity.

label: Moral Beauty
definition: Moral beauty denotes the analogy between virtue's excellence and aesthetic beauty, where virtue is perceived as beautiful in itself. In this shard Cockburn reports Warburton's opponent arguing virtue 'was from its own beauty and excellence, the ultimate end of man,' and that its intrinsic beauty survived the fall, while Watts's Logick discusses beauty, order, and final causes and Pope's Essay treats gradation and order, linking moral and aesthetic perception.

label: Moral Evil
definition: In King's second volume moral evil denotes inconveniencies of life and condition that befall ourselves or others through wrong elections rather than through the necessary order of natural causes. King distinguishes moral evils as those incurred knowingly and with consent, where the agent chooses either the evil itself or what is necessarily connected with it, and argues they flow from misuse of a finite power of choosing. The ensuing analysis treats the nature of elections, how happiness depends upon them, and how such misactions are to be reconciled with divine power and goodness.

label: Moral Fitness
aliases: eternal and necessary Differences of Things
definition: Moral fitness is Clarke's doctrine that good and evil, fitness and unfitness, are eternal and necessary differences in the nature of things, antecedent to will and positive appointment, from which obligations necessarily follow. Contents announce propositions that there are eternal and necessary differences and that the Will of God always determines itself according to the eternal Reason of Things. Opponents who deny such differences are refuted as absurd, and the variety of opinions among nations is answered without conceding relativism.

label: Moral Obligation
definition: Moral obligation for Rutherforth denotes the ground that makes virtuous practice required rather than merely approved, which he denies can be supplied by eternal and necessary differences or by bare fitness and unfitness of things. Rutherforth argues obligation arises only where the practice of virtue connects to the agent's happiness and to divine sanctions, not from abstract relations. The chapter contents explicitly mark fitness theories as insufficient causes of obligation.

label: Moral Sense
aliases: moral sense of beauty and deformity
definition: Hutcheson's internal sense of moral beauty/deformity — approving affections independently of interest. Turnbull: 'moral sense of beauty and deformity in affections.' Fordyce asks 'Whether such a Power belongs' to humans. Rutherforth (1744) is the corpus's principal CRITIC. CAUTION: Chudleigh's 'Celestial Virtues shine' is not moral-sense content.

label: Moral World
definition: Moral world denotes the system of rational agents governed by general laws analogous to natural laws, central to Turnbull's design to reduce moral appearances to general laws. The harmony and beauty of the moral world depends on providential ordering as grain lies dead in winter yet brings forth fruit in season; its seeming non-interposition is defended as regular course like nature. Law's dispensations and Rutherforth's moral world governed by virtue extend the system.

label: Mortification
definition: In Astell's Christian Religion and Norris's Spiritual Counsel mortification is the Christian discipline of living above pleasures of sense and low concerns of the body by privation of sensible pleasure and governance of thoughts, thereby lessening concupiscence and making grace efficacious. Astell distinguishes true mortification from mere bodily austerities and insists it is not transient but a habitual living above sense, pleasant once habitually subjected to mind. Norris makes mortification and self-denial, joined with retreat, solitude, and governing the intellectual frame, the means to further the prevalency of grace after conversion.

label: Natural Affection
definition: Natural affection denotes innate, other-regarding propensities such as parental love and compassion that Hutcheson holds to be as basic as self-love. The texts argue humans are furnished by providence with natural affections that destine them for action and society, opposed to artificial selfish systems. Pope describes these affections extending from self to family to mankind via reflection.

label: Natural Evil
definition: Natural evil denotes suffering arising from the necessary constitution of matter and motion—attrition, corruption and dissolution—distinct from moral evil through wrong elections. King gives the full account of natural evils before tracing moral origin, noting dissolution and attendant evils follow from a self-moving principle. Warburton borrows the concession concerning natural evil to show moral evil promotes good of the whole.

label: Natural Law
definition: Natural law is the system of universal rules discoverable by reason, antecedent to positive institution, governing rights and obligations considered as individuals. Rutherforth distinguishes laws either natural or voluntary, and natural from divine positive laws, organizing his Institutes as lectures on Grotius de Jure Belli et Pacis. He correlates right and obligation under natural law and traces property, contract, and oath to its principles, while Turnbull likewise treats moral philosophy as Newtonian induction to general laws.

label: Natural Religion
definition: Natural religion is the body of unalterable moral obligations incumbent on rational creatures, demonstrable from the being and attributes of God and from natural philosophy without revelation. Clarke's Discourse proves its obligations from eternal Differences of Things and defends Christian revelation as their republication and enforcement, arguing that deistical denials collapse into profanity incapable of argument. Its propositions include that moral obligations are incumbent antecedent to positive institution and to expectation of reward or punishment.

label: Natural Sympathy
definition: Natural sympathy denotes the vital union whereby soul and body mutually suffer, and soul receives information from without by sympathizing with passions of its own body concerning individual bodies round about. Cudworth argues all sense arises from this natural sympathy or compassion with its vitally united body, while Norris's hymn makes Love give Nature her sympathy. The doctrine bridges Cartesian interactionism, moral sense, and theories of providential attachment.

label: Necessity
definition: Metaphysical necessity in the liberty-necessity debate: whether actions are necessitated (King's 'Freedom from Compulsion only, but not from Necessity'), whether necessity excludes moral accountability (Clarke's Remarks against Collins). CAUTION: do not cite everyday 'necessary Caution/Seasons' uses (Burnet) or bookseller advertisements — the concept is the determinism debate.

label: Oath
definition: Oath is the solemn invocation of divine witness to guarantee truth or fidelity, requiring outward circumstances plainly showing intent to swear and inner intention to be bound. Rutherforth treats oaths as implied promises confirmed by calling God as avenger of falsehood, discusses fidelity versus veracity obligations, concealments consistent with veracity, proxy oaths, and whether a pagan's oath by a false god binds. Its security rests on wisdom and power able to search thoughts and exclude from happiness.

label: Obligation
definition: Obligation is the necessitated moral tie arising from eternal and necessary differences of things, incumbent on all rational creatures antecedent to will and to reward or punishment. Clarke's Proposition I states that from those differences there naturally arise certain moral obligations, and Rutherforth makes obligation correlative to right, with natural and voluntary obligations distinguished. Extorted promises, property, and oaths are tested against whether obligation and corresponding right can subsist.

label: Origin of Evil
definition: The origin of evil is the theodicean problem of how pain, sin and imperfection arise under divine providence, focal in King's Essay. King attributes evil to creaturely finitude, free choice and the necessity of laws governing imperfect beings, while respondents debate whether pain inflicted by God is medicinal and compatible with perfect goodness.

label: Parental Authority
definition: In Rutherforth's Institutes parental authority is the natural right parents have over children arising not immediately from generation but from the parental duty that generation entails. It is divided into three stages — absolute direction in infancy, proper authority in the second part of childhood, and honour due in maturity — and grounds the limits of punishment, sale and adoption. The discussion revises Grotius on whether generation alone can explain the incidents of the relation.

label: Passion
definition: Passion in Hutcheson's scheme is a violent, uneasy sensation accompanying desire or aversion, distinguished from calm affection by its tumult and bodily agitation. The Passions treatise classifies love, hatred, joy, sorrow and their species as movements toward perceived good or evil, while King catalogues passions (resentment, generosity, ambition, envy) as modifications of love and hatred whose government determines virtue.

label: Paternal Authority
definition: In Rutherforth's Institutes paternal authority is the natural dominion of parents over children within the family, distinct from civil jurisdiction which arises only by consent. Rutherforth argues that when a child separates from the parent's family paternal authority ends, and the son may even acquire civil jurisdiction over the father while remaining bound by gratitude, whereas Hutcheson notes that without restraint paternal assistance is lost and youth are exposed to infamy when indulgence is allowed to all.

label: Perfect Right
definition: Rutherforth adopts Grotius's distinction: perfect rights are those which may be asserted with rigor, even by employing force, because the thing or action due is fixed and determinate, correlating with perfect obligations. Imperfect rights concern indeterminate expectations of benevolence and charity, giving no strict demand or foundation for reparation, though their violation is still a fault. Confounding the two produces mistakes about damage, honour and justice.

label: Perfection
definition: Perfection is the completed state of a nature attained by exercise and conformity to its end, with restoration to original perfection as religion's great end. Chudleigh warns against wrong notions of perfection that breed vanity, Burnet makes restoring depraved nature to its original perfection the great end of religion, and King defines the greatest perfection and most happy state as attained by exercise, a state where every pleasing thing is done.

label: Pleasure
definition: Pleasure in the shard is the universal object of desire paired with pain as aversion, whose right or wrong understanding determines evil or good. Pope makes self-love and reason aspire to pain their aversion, pleasure their desire, and declares pleasure rightly understood our greatest good, while Mandeville's Lucinda warns that a great man's actions were not because they were good but because they contributed to his pleasure. Johnson maintains it behoves not to confine affections to self-love only and that postponing present interest or pleasure for greater future one is rational and fit when done in conformity to the will of God.

label: Positive Duty
definition: Positive duty for Newcome is a duty not apparent from nature of things but made such by the positive institution and declared will of the institutor, as the Lord's Supper is for Christians by Christ. Its real design, extent and due manner therefore depend entirely upon what the institutor declared, and cannot be inferred a priori to be limited to a few texts; the whole revelation of God's will must be searched, as antecedent laws illuminate later ones.

label: Positive Law
definition: In Hutcheson and Rutherforth positive law is law revealed only by words or writing and instituted by civil constitution, as opposed to natural law discovered by reason observing natures of things. Hutcheson contrasts natural laws discoverable by reason with positive laws revealed by enactment, while Rutherforth treats positive laws as taking custody of bequests and introducing inheritances and as forbidding legislative self-delegation where no positive law of the constitution forbids it.

label: Power
definition: Power denotes active principle, self-moving agency, and divine all-pervading influence that grounds liberty and causation, contrasted with passive property of matter. Watts and Clarke treat power as capacity of intelligent being to determine its own actions and as divine influence that causes gravity in course of providence, while Cudworth treats atheistical fate as denial of such power. The shard debates whether power to act otherwise is essential to agency.

label: Preferred Indifferent
definition: Preferred indifferents are the Stoic technical class of externals that are neither good nor evil but, as Hutcheson's Marcus note explains, are to be pursued according to nature when they do not obstruct proper offices. Marcus is advised to repute obstructing persons among things indifferent no less than sun, wind or savage beast, since they cannot obstruct purpose or disposition because of reservation and power of turning course.

label: Prejudice
definition: Prejudice is a pre-judgment that misleads reasoning before examination of evidence, often inculcated by custom and education. Watts collects 'the chief Principles and Rules of right Judgment in Matters of common and sacred Importance, and pointed out our most frequent Mistakes and Prejudices in the Concerns of Life and Religion, that we might better guard against the Springs of Error.' The logic aims to rescue reasoning powers from frailty, passion, and authority.

label: Prescience
definition: Prescience for Clarke is divine foreknowledge, which Collins confuses as a single attribute entailing necessity. Clarke argues 'The word Prescience being used to signifie Two distinct Attributes or Perfections of the Divine Nature, which, though vulgarly called by the Same common Name, are yet as really and truly different from each other, as any other two Attributes' — prescience of necessary effects via causal chains versus infallible judgment concerning free causes. The latter no more necessitates acts than our judging a contingent truth makes it cease to be contingent.

label: Pride
definition: Pride for Norris denotes the opposed vice whose sinfulness, odiousness, and folly forms the contrarian pole of humility, extended in later chapters to reflections upon the pride of the present age. The table of contents and closing sections treat pride as a habitual esteem inflated beyond desert, related to vain-glory and self-complacency. Norris makes the opposition between humility and pride structural to moral reform.

label: Private Vice
definition: Private vice is Mandeville's term for self-interested frailties that, when skillfully managed by government and honour, are turned to the advantage of civil society and supply the place of moral virtues. The subtitle of the Fable advertises that 'Human Frailties, during the degeneracy of MANKIND, may be turn'd to the Advantage of the CIVIL SOCIETY, and made to supply the Place of Moral Virtues.' The paradox exposes the unreasonableness of expecting an opulent nation to retain golden-age innocence.

label: Private War
definition: For Rutherforth private war is war in the liberty of nature before the institution of civil societies, defined as a contention by force for controversies that can be decided by no other means and not only the act of contending but the state of those determined to use force. It is naturally lawful and its right is only abridged, not wholly taken away, by civil union, informing later limits on defence, reparation and punishment under civil jurisdiction.

label: Probationary State
aliases: state of education, trial, and discipline
definition: Probationary state denotes this life as education, trial and discipline preparing for future reward, a central Turnbull thesis. St Paul's rule for future state implies present state is probationary, a state of education, trial, and discipline in which foundation is laid for after happiness; mixture of evils is necessary to probationary state as proper school for forming and exercising virtues before perfection.

label: Promise
definition: Promise is the declaration that becomes binding only upon acceptance, upon which the promisee acquires a demand and the promiser an obligation. Rutherforth insists a promise after it is made may be recalled before acceptance and distinguishes rash but binding promises where the actor had liberty and understanding. His lectures dissect fear, mistake, unlawfulness, and error as conditions voiding promises, with Grotius as foil.

label: Property
definition: Property is Rutherforth's foundational natural-law institution remedying inconveniences of community of goods, acquired originally by occupancy or compact and divided into general and particular property. His contents trace property from things not appropriated originally, through community of goods, to occupancy, prescription, and restitution, with extreme necessity setting it aside. The law of nature obliges others not to hinder enjoyment of what is one's own, linking property to obligation and justice.

label: Prophecy
definition: Prophecy is divine foretelling of a future event that human power cannot accomplish or that is fulfilled by agents ignorant of it, serving as evidence that the speaker is God's messenger. Newcome distinguishes three grades of prophetic evidence, culminating in concurrence of many characters upon one person, and argues Moses must have plainly foretold the Messiah so belief in Moses entails belief in Jesus. Prophecy and miracle together constitute the twofold evidence for divine revelation.

label: Providence
definition: Divine governance of the world toward ends. TWO strands in the corpus: (1) Turnbull/King's general-law providence — God governs via stable general laws, never-ceasing superintendency; (2) the Stoic-derived moral attitude of accepting one's lot as appointed (Hutcheson p52, Marcus Aurelius). Both are genuine; do not reduce one to the other.

label: Public Good
definition: In Hutcheson's Essay public good denotes the most extensive system to which benevolence reaches, distinct from private good as pleasure. Hutcheson argues perfection of virtue consists in having universal calm benevolence as prevalent affection limiting selfish passions and particular kind affections, with desires toward public good proportioned to moment of the goods when circumstances equal. Norris's third requisite for regulation of self-love is that we will no good to ourselves inconsistent with good of the community, because public good is of greater consequence than private. Rutherforth likewise makes benevolence and justice constitute virtue as doing good or preventing harm.

label: Pulchritude
definition: Pulchritude denotes proportion, symmetry and commensuration of figures and sounds whereby infinity is measured and multiplicity triumphed over, extended from visible objects and harmony to strength and ability of corporeal things. Norris hymns Sovereign Beauty as universal throne to which Stoicks themselves reign, while Cudworth makes beauty and pulchritude depend upon relations and proportions. The shard links pulchritude to virtue's face and to divine exemplarism.

label: Punishment
definition: Punishment denotes the legally appointed pain for crimes, discussed for its proportion, justice and defence of goods. Rutherforth examines whether legislators decreed any capital punishment against theft and notes the Mosaic and Twelve Tables laws, distinguishing night-theft liability from day-theft. The analysis connects punishment to natural law, mercy of laws and threat to liberty.

label: Quaker Light
definition: Quaker Light in Norris's Two Treatises is the Quakers' doctrine that the Light of Christ is a real spiritual substance communicated as a measure of the Spirit to every man, extraordinary and added to common understanding, by which God directs practice. Against Barclay and Vickris, Norris argues the Light is not simply necessary to understanding in general—since Barclay concedes man hath natural reason—but is claimed to be supernaturally given, material-immaterial confusion making it a body like seed or manna. Norris exposes grossness in making Light a material creature and confusion in holding all men capable yet not actually enlightened.

label: Reason
definition: Reason in this corpus is the intellectual power that discerns immutable relations and participates in the divine order, emphasized by Cudworth as an inward active principle that perceives beauty, harmony, and moral signatures beyond bare sense. Norris contrasts reason and love's impetuous motion, noting we love long before we know what it is to love, while Masham defends the use of reasoning and internal discourse to fix affections upon God against the quietist claim to be above reason. The standing question is whether reason or passion is superior in moral judgement.

label: Reason and Faith
definition: Reason and faith are presented as the two greatest perfections of human nature that conspire in eminent persons and in Oxford's colleges as schools of piety and philosophy. Norris's Reason and Religion, or The Grounds and Measures of Devotion Consider'd from the Nature of God and the Nature of Man, assigns contemplations to each nature, insisting God is the most intelligible object, the First Being, First Truth, and therefore most knowable. The work resists resting evident duties on doubtful precarious hypotheses, aligning Masham's caution against basing love of God on Malebranchean occasionalism.

label: Regulation of Love
definition: Regulation of love is Norris's second main task after theory: prescribing measures for directive love as the proper subject of morality rather than mere understanding, because love's acts are transient and leave external effects. For self-love the measures are to love ourselves truly on the whole, not by halves, and not to will ourselves any good inconsistent with the good of the community. For concupiscence the inquiry is what we must desire, what we may desire, and what sensual pleasure may be allowed without intemperance.

label: Religious Practice
definition: Religious practice comprises prayer, devotion, meditation and other duties of religion built upon principles of accountability, immortality and future state. Watts grounds religious practices on accountability and future state, Masham treats formal devotions and solemnities as corrupted when severed from government of reason, and King treats natural evils as occasions for practicing virtue through disciplined devotion rather than speculative complaints.

label: Reparation
definition: In Rutherforth's law of nature reparation is the claim to be made whole for damage done by another's fault, arising only where a perfect right has been violated and some loss or diminution of what is strictly one's own has occurred. An imperfect right, or mere disappointment of benevolent expectation, cannot found a demand for reparation, and the measure of damages includes both the thing and its fruits. The doctrine links justice, property and the role of civil jurisdiction.

label: Resignation
definition: Resignation is the Christian-Stoic acquiescence to Providence with firm persuasion that divine Orders are best, proposed as true Heroism in Law (p22) alongside Humility, Meekness and Benevolence under severe temptations. Astell (p110) commends Precepts and Providence, acquiescing in all His Orders (p110), while Masham's letters test Stoic resignation against affliction, concluding quiet and contentment is most Stoical (p25) and that Stoic indifference must be balanced with sociability.

label: Revelation
definition: Revelation is God's supernatural communication of truths concerning his will and the future state that natural reason, though sufficient as a rule of natural religion, cannot securely establish in mankind's present corrupted condition. Campbell argues laws of nature are a certain rule to happiness yet do not supersede supernatural Revelation, Warburton defends Revelation's projected necessity, Clarke brackets Revelation to argue from reason alone against those who acknowledge no authority but reason, and Masham faults instructors who suppose recipients already convinced of Revelation's authority without prior rational conviction.

label: Reward and Punishment
definition: Reward and punishment in Johnson and Clarke are the sanctions that alone render a law obligatory, with Johnson following Locke that God enforces his law by rewards and punishments of infinite weight and duration in another life and that no one can take us out of his hands. Johnson defines a law as including obligation in its very idea, and obligation as founded upon rewards and punishments supposing a superior. Clarke argues his proof of immateriality is useful precisely because it establishes possibility of a future state of rewards and punishments against Dodwell's mortalism.

label: Ridicule
definition: Ridicule in Astell's Enquiry after Wit is proposed by Shaftesbury's Letter Concerning Enthusiasm as an infallible test to expose imposture and enthusiasm, applicable to any subject. Astell retorts that no ridicule can lie against reason or rational religion, which is improv'd reason, and that the rule turns absurd when applied to grave and truly important matters, becoming mere Buffoonery that undermines reverence without providing a consistent system in its place.

label: Ruling Passion
definition: Pope's ruling passion in Epistle II is a single dominant passion, arising with the body's humours and imagination, that subordinates all other passions as Aaron's serpent swallowed the rest. Received at birth as the mind's disease, it grows with growth and strength with strength, directing character and explaining human consistency and contradiction, and becomes the key to mastering and governing the self.

label: Sacrament
definition: In Newcome's 1737 critique, the sacrament of the Lord's Supper is a positive institution made a duty to Christians by the declared will of its institutor, not a duty apparent from the nature of things.
