She argues against Hoadly's Plain Account that its nature, design and acceptable manner of performance must be sought in the whole revelation of God, not in a few select New Testament texts alone, requiring moral qualifications such as charity and sincerity.

label: Sacramental Remembrance
definition: The doctrine that remembering Christ's sacrifice is essential to worthy sacrament reception. Newcome grants remembrance is 'an essential and necessary part of this Duty' but DENIES it is the END of the institution (contra Hoadly), insisting on antecedent moral qualifications as the ground of worthy reception.

label: Sacrifice and Atonement
definition: Sacrifice and atonement is Law's account of Christ's work not as equivalent satisfaction but as a divinely appointed and accepted scheme of government, a merciful expedient securing the ends of law and satisfying its intention. Propitiatory sacrifice, ransom, and buying are biblical metaphors for this moral constitution; redemption rests on Christ's whole ministry and universal righteousness opposed to Adam's sin, not on a single act, and is freely appointed by God's wisdom as supreme Governor.

label: Scale of Being
definition: The scale or chain of being denotes gradated hierarchy of beings from mites to man to God via increasing reason and perfections. Watts invokes high Degrees of Reason in beasts to suggest probable souls above, Hutcheson invokes connexion and mutual dependencies as evidence of one Cause ordering the scale, and Pope figures benevolent expansion from centre to whole worlds as systematically grasping that scale.

label: Scripture
definition: Scripture is the divinely inspired text containing God's revealed will, to be searched as oracle for what God requires to be believed and done. Masham urges referral to Scriptures themselves after establishing revelation's authority as the clearest rational evidence. Warburton fears being charged as warmer advocate for doctor than Scripture. Clarke formally brackets testimony from Scripture to argue demonstratively from reason alone against atheists.

label: Self-Command
definition: In Turnbull's Observations self-command is the cultivated habit of bringing affections to trial by a considered standard and restraining present inclination for the superior pleasure of doing good and gaining approbation of reason. It is formed by inuring children early to bear and forbear, to obey reason and to place ambition in merit, and is described as true power, dominion and greatness of soul without which one lives tumultuously. Masham and King connect its failure to the ill principle and necessity of imperfect will.

label: Self-Examination
definition: Self-examination is the daily practice of interrogating animal powers and the governing part recommended by Marcus (via Hutcheson) and Shaftesbury and codified by Burnet's devotional rule. Marcus asks to what purposes animal powers are used and what sort of soul one has — child, youth, tyrant, beast — while Shaftesbury makes it the preparatory discipline for authors, Turnbull links it to self-conversation and self-command, and Burnet titles a devotional section Of Self-Examination.

label: Self-Government
definition: Self-government is the exercise of rational command over particular passions by cultivating calm, general desires through reflection and habit. Hutcheson presents it as strengthening universal benevolence to overpower turbulent affections, while Burnet frames it as surrendering liberty to divine direction, asking God to destroy sinful self-will and work right willing.

label: Self-Knowledge
definition: Self-knowledge in Norris denotes the immediate foundation of humility, expressed as having a true and just sense of ourselves and thinking truly about what we are. Norris records the rarity of humility as evidence that very few indeed know themselves to any purpose, while inculcating knowledge of ourselves as the general principle of morality and the primary radical notion out of which humility grows. The doctrine connects anthropology with methodical self-examination across the whole life.

label: Self-Love
definition: Self-love as the natural inclination to one's own preservation and happiness — distinguished from selfish vice and compatible with benevolence. Pope: 'true Self-love and Social are the same'; Hutcheson treats it as ultimate motive alongside benevolence; the central debate (Shaftesbury/Mandeville/Hutcheson/Butler/Cockburn) is whether self-love is the sole spring of action.

label: Self-Moving Power
definition: Self-moving power for Clarke is the active principle inhering in an intelligent substance by which it freely exerts agency as the proper physical and immediate cause of motion, distinct from passive perception or abstract motives. Reasons, motives, pleasure and pain are only occasions upon which the self-moving substance acts, never the efficient cause; denying this power reduces men to necessary agents like clocks, and makes agency contradictory.

label: Self-Preservation
definition: Self-preservation is the fundamental inclination to preserve one's own being and right use of faculties, treated as a first law of nature that grounds duties to self and to others. Clarke argues every man is bound to preserve his own being as far as in him lies, and Hobbes's reduction of all obligation to self-preservation is criticized as making the easiest course to cut off others, contradicting natural differences of right. Hutcheson and Pope relate self-preservation to self-love as its more urgent mode, distinct from benevolent affections.

label: Seneca
definition: Seneca is cited in the shard as Stoic authority on time and on the alternation of solitude and company, and as source for critiques of prodigality and for moral maxims about perfect happiness. Norris invokes Seneca's dictum that time alone merits covetousness to censure prodigality of time, and Latin tags Mifienda & alternanda sunt Solitudo & Frequentia and Quousque eadem to prescribe study, meditation and devotion. The citations exemplify how Neostoic Latinity mediates Christian moral psychology.

label: Seneca Reference
definition: Explicit citation of Lucius Annaeus Seneca in the corpus, used both as stylistic comparison (Gwinnett's 'Laconic' style likened to Seneca) and as shared intellectual canon (Drake lists Seneca with Plutarch and Cicero as resources for women readers) and as a scholarly footnote (King cites Seneca Ep. 24 on providence). The citations show Seneca remains a live authority for ethics and natural religion, contrary to assumption that Lipsius is the sole Stoic mediator.

label: Sensus Communis
definition: Sensus communis in Shaftesbury denotes the natural affection for community and public weal, reclaimed from Roman satirists via Casaubon and Gataker glosses, and posited as the Essay on the Freedom of Wit and Humour's ethical foundation. Hutcheson's Introduction explains Shaftesbury's discovery of its true sense as love of community and natural equality, distinct from vulgar common sense, while Turnbull catalogues it among the moral senses alongside sensus decori and pulchri.

label: Shame
definition: Shame is the painful sense of dishonour or ignominy that serves as punishment for vice, the reverse of honour as reward. Mandeville defines 'The Reverse of Honour is Dishonour or Ignominy, which consists in the bad Opinion and Contempt of others, and as the first is counted a Reward for good Actions, so this is esteem'd a Punishment for bad ones... This Ignominy is likewise called Shame.' Hutcheson lists shame with honour and pity as self-interested motives overlying benevolence.

label: Slavery
definition: Slavery is deployed chiefly by Chapone as an analogy for coverture: the hardships of the English laws in relation to wives are said to put wives in a worse condition than slavery itself, making slaves in Turkey a comparative benchmark for English wives' lack of redress. The image of marriage as a state of captivity, borrowed from civil-law revival of wills after captivity, is extended to argue that surviving wives should regain will-making freedom as captives regaining liberty. The trope links domestic law to broader discourses of liberty and arbitrary power.

label: Slavery and Subjection
definition: Slavery and subjection contrast the slave bound to make the good of his master the end of all his actions with the subject bound to preserve civil community's good. Rutherforth argues the master has right to direct all actions of the slave for his own benefit, and the civil despot the right to direct subjects' actions relating to general good; slavery under arbitrary power that destroys property puts legislators into state of war with people absolved from obedience. Turnbull warns against degrading nature into slavery to impure passions.

label: Sociability
definition: Sociability is the natural disposition to live in society that Masham treats as indispensable despite Stoic praise of withdrawal. The editorial summary stresses her lifelong commitment to sociability as basis of happy life requiring balance with detachment. Cockburn similarly argues human happiness is found in that of others via social affections.

label: Soliloquy
definition: Soliloquy denotes Shaftesbury's disciplined practice of self-conversation and private self-examination, posed as the qualifying method for authors and moral agents. In Advice to an Author and the Inquiry, it requires divided self-dialogue to inspect fancy and affection; Hutcheson appropriates Marcus's meditations as exemplary soliloquies, and Turnbull prescribes Marcus and Epictetus as models of self-conversation necessary to self-command and true wisdom.

label: Soul
definition: The soul is debated as either naturally immortal immaterial substance or naturally mortal material system made immortal by superadded spirit at baptism. Clarke defends natural immortality to secure personal identity for resurrection and future rewards, while Dodwell contends the natural soul dies with the body and immortality is adventitious. The soul's power to move the hand by mere preference figures in liberty arguments.

label: Space
definition: In Watts's Philosophical Essays space is the familiar idea of extension void of matter capable of receiving body, debated as to whether it is something or nothing, a substance or mode, God or creature. The table of contents frames the inquiry as 'Is Space Something or Nothing?', 'Is Space a Substance?', and 'Space cannot be God,' and the text discovers that philosophers divide between depressing space to nothing and exalting it to divinity.

label: Spirit
definition: Spirit is defined by Watts as a thinking, self-subsisting being whose essence is cogitation, not extension, and whose duration is measured by succession of ideas. The shard treats spirit as the subject of consciousness, immortality, and moral agency, capable of knowing God, honouring or dishonouring the Maker, and persisting beyond bodily dissolution.

label: State of Nature
definition: State of nature denotes the condition before civil union where every individual is his own master with independent sovereign power over himself. Rutherforth argues each individual who associates forms civil society to obtain assistance for maintenance of rights, expecting in return to agree to what is necessary for common benefit; absent members may vote by proxy and natural majority governs where equality deadlocks. Turnbull treats natural sociability and instincts as provision for this state.

label: Stoic Apathy
definition: Astell explicitly rejects Stoical Apathy as the ground of Christian contentment, contrasting it with a Rational Conviction that the soul is under the all-wise government and care of infinite goodness. Real religious tranquility is not insensibility of pain as the Stoics vainly boasted of their wise man, but cheerful acceptance of providence through reason. Turnbull invokes the historical Stoics — Diodatus the stoic, Zeno and Possidonius — as models of logic and moral discipline behind Cicero's formation.

label: Stoic Discipline
definition: Stoic discipline is the practice of resigning will to universal nature, keeping the governing part calm and well-pleased, central to Hutcheson's Marcus translation. The Inner Citadel context and Gataker's Praeloquium title comparing Stoics with Peripatetics, Old Academics and more especially with the modern systems, frame Marcus as Stoic exemplar. Marcus is advised to love even those who offend as kindred by nature and to display the soul pleased with all the Gods appoint, cordially assenting rather than barely obeying.

label: Stoic Fate
definition: The Stoic doctrine of fate as discussed and differentiated from the author's own account of liberty and necessity. Clarke reports the Stoic view that souls, though divine, may be 'immersed in Sense' and liable to misery, while King argues the ancient Stoics held the same liberty conception as his own (freedom as power of contrary choice within limits) but without distinct explanation. Gwinnett dramatizes a 'rigid Stoick' who despises argument, showing the popular literary stereotype of Stoic impassivity.

label: Stoic Indifference
definition: Stoic indifference is the cultivated detachment that treats society, friendship and fortune as neither good nor bad but indifferents, the perfection of reason being the sole good pursued unconditionally. Masham's early letters stage the dialectic: a Christianized-Stoic philosophy of withdrawal (p5) vs sociability, and the trial to turne a Stoick (p22) and live with Stoical sort of Indifference (p39) despite finding herself Divided into as many Parts as there are Persons she loves. Astell (p231) retorts that Stoicks despis'd Riches in Words tho' they had Hundred Thousands at Use, exposing vain-glory, while Gwinnett dramatizes a rigid Stoic interlocutor.

label: Stoic and Senecan Reception
definition: Stoic and Senecan reception is the 18th-century use of Stoic exempla and texts for moral formation, especially Seneca's Morals and Panetian virtue division. Balfour cites Cicero's borrowing from Panetius the Stoic and Seneca's Providence comparing Regulus and Mæcenas and the Stoic-eyed Mornay in Voltaire, while Chudleigh recommends Seneca's Morals next to Scripture for learning to bear providential ills with indifference. The search found no occurrence of Justus Lipsius, the early-modern Stoic revivalist, across all 612 pages of this shard.

label: Stoic Virtue
definition: Stoic virtue is the boast that an innocent creature pursuing virtue with utmost power may in virtue equal the gods, formalized by Hutcheson as M/A = Unity where motive equals ability. Hutcheson grants this as the only foundation for Stoic equality but confines it to innocence and infinite ability, while Law's Pharisees/Stoics/Epicureans as perverse disputers and Cockburn's dramatic probity offer non-Stoic alternatives.

label: Stoicism
definition: The reception of Stoic philosophy in 18th-c British moral philosophy: Astell's citations of Epictetus/Seneca, Shaftesbury's Stoic discipline, Turnbull's 'Stoic philosopher' references, Cudworth's 'Stoical Fate,' and Chudleigh's 'Their Apathy let Stoicks still admire.' Distinct from: classical_stoicism (the ancient doctrine itself) and stoic_apathy (the specific passion-indifference doctrine).

label: Subordination
definition: Subordination denotes the hierarchical relation of the Son to the Father in Clarke's Trinitarian theology and, analogically, of creatures to God and to one another in Pope's chain. In this shard Clarke's Scripture Doctrine collects passages 'wherein is expressed the Subordination of the Son to the Father; his deriving his Being, Glory and Powers, from Him' while Pope's Essay and Watts's Logick use subordination to describe order and gradation in creation.

label: Substance
definition: Substance in Watts denotes the two only proper substances we know—body as solid extension and spirit as thinking power—with dispute over whether the name applies to space and how to distinguish material from immaterial being. Watts allocates distinct considerations to solid extension and thinking power, arguing clear ideas of their distinct essences provide the clue to visible and invisible worlds.

label: Superstition
definition: Superstition denotes false religion compounded of enthusiastic imagination and terrifying opinion, contrasted by Shaftesbury and Hutcheson with philosophical theism and true devotion. Shaftesbury maps it as a modification of enthusiasm persisting via priestcraft; Hutcheson treats heathen worship as full of ridiculous superstitions lacking evidence, while Burnet and Astell prescribe devotion and toleration as cures for superstitious fear.

label: Syllogism
definition: Syllogism is Watts's third operation of the mind, joining several propositions to infer the less known from the more evident. The Third Part of Logick defines its nature, parts, and kinds with rules, contrasting sharp syllogistic reasoning with the imprudent custom of talking Pro and Con in schools.

label: Syllogistic Method
definition: Syllogistic method denotes the academic rules governing logical disputation, especially the respondent's duties to repeat the opponent's argument verbatim, detect formal faults, and show failure to oppose the thesis. In this shard Watts's Improvement (part 2) codifies 'The Laws that oblige the Respondent' and 'If the Syllogism be false in the Logical Form' and warns against determining large questions by a single argument, while his Logick furnishes varieties of rules to guard against error.

label: Sympathy
definition: Sympathy is the mutual responsiveness linking soul and body and generating uneasy benevolent passions at another's misery. King notes the soul and body admit of a mutual sympathy requiring care of the body, Warburton treats sympathy of another's misery as a passion, and Campbell describes the uneasy benevolent passion as universally called a pleasing anguish, a generous sympathy.

label: Taste
definition: Taste in Turnbull's Education for Life is the cultivated sense of beauty, order and decorum that links liberal arts, morals and painting, distinguished into fine versus false learning. The Preface seeks 'to lead young Gentlemen... into a juster Notion of the Fine Arts than is commonly entertained... by distinguishing the fine Taste of them from the false Learning that too frequently passes for it.' Taste shares the same object, rule and measure in science, arts and life — imitation of nature — and is improveable by education.

label: Time
definition: Time in the shard denotes a precious revenue dealt out in minutes and little parcels, whose prodigality is censured via Seneca and whose husbanding is a cardinal prudential precept, and a deficient cause structure in Watts's ontology. Norris, following Seneca, argues time alone merits covetousness, while Watts treats duration as measured by succession of ideas and links want of time or forgetfulness to deficient causation. Time thus connects prudence, consciousness, and causation.

label: Toleration
definition: Toleration is the legal permission of separate congregations intended to preserve peace and liberty of conscience. Astell argues that by being very careful to preserve an Act of Toleration the minds of the people are set at quiet and the measures of separate congregations are broken, whereas persecution revives zeal. The discussion situates toleration between arbitrary power, national interest, and the security of the established church.

label: Trinity
definition: The Trinity denotes the doctrine of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three persons, whose scriptural warrant and metaphysical coherence Clarke examines by collecting and comparing all New Testament texts. In this shard Clarke's Scripture Doctrine (1712) surveys every New Testament passage relating to the Trinity and the liturgy, arguing for subordination of the Son and Spirit to the Father against Arians and Socinians, while Cockburn's Works engage the same controversy via her defence of Clarke's fitness account.

label: Tyranny
definition: Tyranny as the inversion of lawful rule into arbitrary power, triggering resistance theory. Drake casts male dominance as 'by their Tyranny their Rule maintain'd' until deposed by Wit, paralleling political usurpation. Rutherforth makes the people's right 'of forcibly resisting the tyranny of civil governours' the test case for whether popular resistance is superior or inferior to supreme power, and catalogs tyranny and oppression as the social pathology that dissolves civil union's ends.

label: University Education
definition: University education denotes Shaftesbury's program for a young nobleman at Oxford, where Several Letters guides the youth's reading and judgment against enthusiasm and custom. The Philosophical Regimen complements it with the Stoic regimen of self-examination and care of education undertaken by the grandfather, showing that good literature and early discipline form the university youth's character rather than mere school custom.

label: Vice
definition: Vice in Balfour and Burnet is the corruption of nature displayed when instinct or passion is not regulated by reason and reflection, leading to conduct pernicious to self and society. Balfour warns that vice frequently insinuates itself with an immediate smile and present gratifications that flatter judgment. Clarke and Mandeville connect vice to atheistical corruption of manners and to physiology of passions.

label: Virginity
definition: Virginity is the central female virtue dramatized in Mandeville's Mysteries of Virginity, whose dialogues oppose Lucinda and Antonia on whether reservedness preserves liberty or invites ruin. Lucinda warns that she that listens to seduction is ruined and her liberty lost, and satirizes modern Virgins as temples of modesty going bare-arsed while affecting singularity. Mandeville notes hardly one in fifty keeps virginity past forty unless dying young, yet old maids who kept it rejoice at preserved liberty while married women repent the yoke.

label: Virtue
definition: Virtue denotes the habitual performance of duty to self, society and God, constituting moral excellence and true happiness. Fordyce structures his Elements around the principal Distinction of Duty or Virtue and its threefold duties, while Turnbull proves the Christian doctrine concerning God, Providence, Virtue and a Future State to be agreeable to true philosophy. Virtue is presented as both present happiness and the object of divine legislation requiring habit and education.

label: Virtue and Atheism
definition: Virtue and atheism poses whether virtuous character can subsist without religion, a test case for Warburton's alliance theory and Law's exemplarism. Warburton catalogues the partisan abuse of liberty where opponents figure alternately as superstitious bigots and as a cabal of mere politiques, tartufes without religion, atheists in black gowns, apostates without faith or law. Against mere political virtue of reputation, Law holds Christ's condescending example, not party virtue that dare oppose extremes, as the public blessing that alone reforms manners durably.

label: War
definition: In Rutherforth's Institutes (Chap. XIX) war is defined as a contention by force, signifying not only an act but a state or condition of those determined to decide a controversy by force, distinguished into private war between private persons and public war between public persons (bodies politic). In the liberty of nature individuals may lawfully make war to defend goods, recover reparation, and insist punishment when injury cannot otherwise be prevented; the right of private war is abridged but not wholly taken away by civil society.

label: Will
definition: Will is the appetitive power whose conformity to the dictates of understanding raises the classic worry about liberty, since if dictates are wholly necessary the will's necessary conformity would leave no Tò eph' hemin. Norris treats will alongside sensitive desire, noting intellectual versus sensitive appetites can conspire or divide, producing the contention between flesh and spirit. Cudworth's dialectic places will between intellect and bodily appetite, testing whether advertency furnishes the seat of free agency.

label: Wisdom
definition: Wisdom is the intellectual virtue of rightly ordering knowledge and choice, treated as the highest perfection of governing power. Chudleigh pairs wisdom with conscience as the only truly desirable applause, Burnet makes sincere self-knowledge the foundation of all true wisdom and virtue, and King and Warburton frame creation's present state as the highest instance of infinite wisdom, power and goodness, with infinite wisdom forming the best of all possible systems.

label: Wit
definition: For Astell in Bart'lemy Fair (1709), wit is the fashionable faculty of raillery and ridicule that enthusiasts elevate to a test of truth, contrasted with judgment, reason, and true good humour. Drawing on Locke, she shows wit chiefly considers appearances rather than truth, and becomes dangerous when joined with power, while true wit must be distinguished from buffoonery, pannic transports, and enthusiasm that threatens religion and manners.

label: Wit and Humour
definition: Wit and humour are, for Shaftesbury, the proper test of truth and the instrument of Sensus Communis, the freedom to canvass opinions sociably. Characteristicks pairs 'Sensus Communis; an Essay on the Freedom of Wit and Humour' with Letter Concerning Enthusiasm, arguing that men are accountable only for actions at first, but when magistrates become dressers imposing uniform intellectual complexions, free wit exposes imposture. The essay defends raillery against alleged enemies of ridicule who would silence it on certain subjects from mistrust of their own judgment.
